questions.q: **REMEMBER:** What is the definition of “theme” in a literary text?
questions.a:
The theme is the central idea or underlying message that the author explores through the story, characters, and events.  
A wrong answer such as “the theme is the setting of the story” reveals the student confuses theme with setting, indicating they need to revisit how theme differs from story elements like time and place.

questions.q: **UNDERSTAND:** In your own words, explain how sacrifice is shown when Major Sharma refuses to leave his post.
questions.a:
Sacrifice is shown because Major Sharma chooses to stay and fight, knowing he may die, rather than retreat to save himself.  
If a student answers “He was brave because he fought hard,” they focus only on bravery and miss the element of giving up personal safety, showing they do not yet link bravery to the concept of sacrifice.

questions.q: **APPLY:** Using the idea of duty, identify one sentence from the text that illustrates Major Sharma’s sense of duty and explain why it fits.
questions.a:
Sentence: “I will not withdraw but will fight till the last man and the last round.”  
Explanation: This sentence shows duty because he states his obligation to hold the position regardless of personal cost, reflecting his commitment to his role as an officer.  
A wrong answer that picks a line about the weather and says it shows duty reveals the student cannot distinguish relevant evidence, indicating they need practice locating textual support for abstract concepts.

questions.q: **ANALYZE:** Compare how the themes of patriotism and duty are interrelated in Major Sharma’s decision to defend the airfield.
questions.a:
Patriotism fuels his love for the nation, making him want to protect the airfield; duty translates that love into concrete action—he follows orders and his oath to defend the post. Together, patriotism provides the motivation, duty provides the responsibility, and the action demonstrates both.  
If a student answers “Patriotism and duty are the same thing,” they fail to see the distinction between feeling (patriotism) and obligation (duty), showing they need to analyze how internal drives become external responsibilities.

questions.q: **EVALUATE:** Judge whether the theme of sacrifice in this chapter is presented as noble or foolish, using evidence from the text to support your judgment.
questions.a:
The theme is presented as noble: Sharma’s sacrifice prevents the airfield from falling, which would have jeopardized the defense of Srinagar. The text notes his actions “saved the airfield and bought time for reinforcements,” indicating his sacrifice had strategic value.  
If a student claims the sacrifice was foolish because he died, they ignore the outcome and the text’s emphasis on the impact of his act, revealing they evaluate based only on personal loss rather than consequential reasoning.

questions.q: **CREATE:** Write a short diary entry (3‑4 sentences) from the perspective of a soldier who witnessed Major Sharma’s last stand, expressing how the themes of sacrifice, patriotism, and duty affected you.
questions.a:
Sample answer:  
“Today I saw Major Sharma refuse to leave our post, even when the enemy surrounded us. His words, ‘I will not withdraw,’ reminded me why we serve—not for glory but for our country. I felt a deep pride (patriotism) and a stronger sense of duty to hold the line. His sacrifice taught me that true courage means putting the nation before self.”  
A poor answer that merely repeats the plot without personal reflection or thematic connection shows the student cannot create original work that applies the concept.
